title: Import flows for a tool people already use
metaTitle: CSV imports that show the failed rows
excerpt: Show a sample file, name the columns that matter, and list the rows that failed. A silent import failure gets blamed on the whole product.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. The paired views fit a piece about showing what an import contains and what it missed.
caption: Show the file you expect, and the rows that did not land. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a CSV import show before the upload?
faqs.answer: A sample file with a few realistic rows, plus a list of which columns are required. The sample should include the formats that usually break, such as dates and values that contain commas. Say whether a second upload updates matching rows or adds duplicates.

faqs.question: How should failed import rows be reported?
faqs.answer: Name the row, the column, the value you saw, and what you needed instead. Give a count of what succeeded and what failed, and offer the failed rows as a file they can fix. A red cell without a sentence, or a single "import failed" when most rows landed, hides the result.

faqs.question: Why does a quiet import failure matter so much?
faqs.answer: The import is often the first time someone trusts the product with real work. If the screen returns to empty, they assume the product lost the file. Show a status, a count, and the bad rows so the failure stays inside the import instead of spreading to the whole tool.

markdown:
A csv import ux has to show a sample file, name the columns that matter, and list the rows that failed. People already keep their work in a spreadsheet or another tool. If the import dies quietly, they will decide the whole product is unreliable, because the first real task never arrived.

Treat the import as a feature with a result, not as a file picker. The person should be able to say, afterward, how many rows landed, how many need a fix, and where the fixed file goes.

## Show a sample before you ask for theirs

Put a real sample next to the upload. A few rows, the same columns you accept, filled with the kind of values you actually parse. A header-only template teaches the column names and hides the formats. Dates, empty cells, and names with commas are where imports break. The sample should contain one of each, with a note beside the file that says what those cells are doing.

Say which columns are required and which are optional, in a list they can read without opening the file. Required means the row cannot land without it. Optional means you will store it if it is present and skip it if it is blank. If a column is required only when another column is set, say that in one sentence under the list. Hidden dependencies are how a file that "matches the template" still fails.

Name the encoding and the separator you expect if you accept anything other than a plain comma-separated file. If you also accept an export from a named tool, say the tool and the menu path that produces a file you have tested. "Export from Settings, then Data" is a better instruction than "use a CSV." Link the sample download in the same block. People should not have to hunt a help article to learn the shape of a file you are about to demand.

Keep the sample in the product, versioned with the importer. When you add a column, update the sample in the same change. A sample from last year is a trap for the person who did what you asked.

## Say which columns matter, then map them

After the upload, show their header row against yours. If the names match, say so and let them continue. If they do not, show a mapping: their column on one side, your field on the other, with anything unmatched marked as skipped.

Do this before you write a single record. A preview of the first few rows, after mapping, lets them see that "Cust Name" landed in the name field and that a date survived. The preview is the moment they can still back out without a mess to undo.

Guess the mapping when the names are close, and show the guess as a guess. Let them change it. An automatic match that is wrong and silent will duplicate or blank a field across hundreds of rows, and the cleanup will be blamed on the product.

State the limits in the same view. Maximum rows, maximum file size, and what you do with extra columns. Extra columns can be ignored on purpose. Say "we will not import these" and list them. Dropping them without a sentence feels like data loss.

If the product can only identify people by email, say that email is the key. A second import should update a row when the email matches, and add a row when it does not. Tell them which behavior you built. "Import" that sometimes duplicates and sometimes overwrites, with no sentence either way, is how a founder spends a weekend in a spreadsheet again.

## Show the rows that failed

Run the check, then show a result that can be read in under a minute. How many rows succeeded. How many failed. A table of the failures: row number, the column, the value you saw, and what you needed instead.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes the guidelines as a shared standard for making web content more accessible, organized under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An import error has to be understandable. WCAG's error-identification criterion asks that when an input error is detected, the item in error is identified and described in text. A red cell with no sentence fails that bar, and it also fails the founder who is not looking at color. Name the row. Name the field. Say what is wrong.

Offer the failed rows as a download that matches the shape of the original file, with a column that explains the problem. They can fix that smaller file and send it back. Making them re-upload the entire original, including the rows you already accepted, creates duplicates unless your update rule is solid. If you do require the full file again, repeat the update rule on the result screen.

Partial success needs a plain status. "412 imported, 18 need a fix" is a finished step. "Import failed" when most of the file landed is a lie that sends people into a second upload. "Import succeeded" when 18 rows were dropped is the quieter lie, and it is the one that gets discovered in front of a customer.

Keep the result until they dismiss it, and keep a record an admin can open later. Imports happen once, under time pressure, often by someone who will not be the person answering questions next month. The record should say who ran it, when, the file name, and the counts.

## What silent failure does to trust

An import that fails silently will be blamed on the whole product. The person did the brave thing: they moved their real work. If the screen returns to an empty state, they have two theories. The product lost the file. Or their data was not worth keeping. Both theories end in a spreadsheet, and in a note to the teammate who suggested the tool.

Spinner forever is a silent failure with motion. Give the job a state: queued, checking, writing, done. If it will take more than a few seconds, say so, and let them leave the page. A finished job should meet them with the same result screen, not a toast that vanishes while they are in another tab.

Timeouts and size limits are failures you can describe. "This file has 20,000 rows and this import accepts 5,000. Split it, or write to us and we will run it with you." That sentence is a product decision. A generic error code is a support ticket you have chosen to have.

Do not "fix" data you do not understand. Trimming a name is fine to mention. Rewriting a date from one format into another is fine if you show the before and after in the preview. Inventing a missing email, or dropping a row because a phone number looked short, needs to be a visible failure, not a kindness in the parser.

## The second import and the undo

People import twice. The first file was a test. The second is the real one. Your rules have to survive that.

Say whether a second run adds, updates, or refuses. Put the choice on the screen before they confirm, with the count of rows that would update and the count that would be new. A preview that only shows brand-new rows hides the overwrites.

Undo belongs in the result, for a defined window, if you can truly reverse it. "Undo" that leaves half the rows behind is worse than no undo. If you cannot reverse, say so before they confirm: "This will add 412 records. You can delete them from the list afterward." Then make that deletion possible, including a filter for "added by the import on this date."

Empty files, files with only a header, and files in the wrong format each get their own sentence. They are different problems. A single "we could not read this file" teaches them nothing to change.

## A check before you call the import done

Sit with a file that is almost right.

- A required column missing.
- A date in the wrong order.
- A name that contains a comma.
- A duplicate of a record already in the product.
- A second run of the same file.
- A file larger than the limit.

For each one, you should be able to point at a sentence on screen that names the situation and the next action. If the only record of the failure is in a server log, the feature is not done. The person with the file cannot see the log, and they will not wait while someone reads it to them.

Watch someone who did not build the importer try the sample, then their own export from the tool they already use. Note every moment they ask "did it work?" That question is a missing count, a missing preview, or a missing failure row.

## After the rows have landed

A good import ends in the product, on the records, with the count still visible. Invite them to open one row and confirm a field they care about. Then leave them to the work. A celebratory modal that blocks the list is a delay.

The next design choice is what the product is allowed to say once people are inside it. [Notifications that earn their interruption](/blog/notifications-that-earn-their-interruption) is the next piece, because a product that pings for its own activity gets muted, including the ping that would have explained a finished import.

The same care shows up in the projects we ship. See [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for interfaces where a task has a visible result. An import is one of those tasks.
